newsitem.title: UK: Britain staged Grand National despite bomb threats.
newsitem.headline: Britain staged Grand National despite bomb threats.

text.p: Britain allowed the rescheduled Grand National steeplechase to go ahead last month in the presence of then Prime Minister John Major, Princess Anne and 20,000 others despite IRA bomb warnings, a newspaper reported on Sunday.
The story in the Mail on Sunday was partially confirmed by police on Merseyside, north-west England.
On April 5, the Saturday set for this year's race, police received telephone calls from people using an Irish Republican Army codeword warning bombs had been planted on the Aintree racecourse.
Some 70,000 racegoers were evacuated, many of them abandoning their cars and being forced to spend the night in hotels, while police undertook a massive search of the course, finding nothing.

But the authorities, determined that the IRA, a guerrilla group which demands the end of British rule in Northern Ireland, should not force cancellation of the event, decided it should be run on April 7 despite the smaller crowd expected on a Monday.
But the Mail on Sunday said that as many as 25 bomb warnings were received in advance of the rescheduled race, some of them accompanied by an IRA codeword.
Despite this, police, who were checking everyone and everything moving into Aintree, decided the race should go ahead, the newspaper reported.
"We became aware of a number of threats. Each one was evaluated, assessed and acted upon without compromising the safety of the public," a police spokesman said.
Major, in the middle of an election campaign, made a surprise appearance at Aintree with his wife Norma, as did Princess Anne, the only daughter of Queen Elizabeth and a keen horsewoman.
The Grand National, one of the most celebrated events in Britain's horseracing calendar, is televised in countries around the world.

The Mail on Sunday quoted the course's managing director Charles Barnett as saying: "The Grand National is a hugely important international sporting event, one of the 10 most important in the world...It had to go on."
